sources.entry: RFC: Propeller: A frame work for Post Link Optimizations - States the design, not a result: basic-block sections and a relink, no binary rewrite, so layout needs no disassembly.

summary.title: [RFC] Propeller: A frame work for Post Link Optimizations
summary.one_liner: Google's llvm-dev RFC proposing Propeller, a scalable, distributed-build-friendly post-link optimizer that does whole-program basic block layout at link time using basic block sections and sampled profiles, instead of rewriting the binary like BOLT.
keywords: how to optimize binary layout after linking
takeaways: Propeller performs whole-program basic block layout at link time by giving each basic block its own section, letting the linker reorder blocks, split functions, and reorder functions.
Its design avoids BOLT's monolithic disassemble-and-rewrite approach, so it works with distributed builds and has lower memory and time overhead.
The workflow is: build with -fpropeller-label, profile with perf LBR samples, convert the profile with create_llvm_prof, then rebuild with -fpropeller-optimize=<profile>.
The linker uses the Ex-TSP block ordering algorithm and needs linker relaxations for jumps; CFI bloat from lack of discontiguous address range support is an open issue.
summary.summary: This mailing-list RFC from Google introduces Propeller, a post-link optimization system for LLVM. Google reports that BOLT improved already ThinLTO+PGO-optimized benchmarks by 2% to 6%, but BOLT's monolithic design had high memory use (about 70G for a ~300M text binary) and long rewrite times. Propeller instead uses basic block sections so the linker can reorder blocks at link time, guided by perf LBR profiles and the Ex-TSP algorithm. The post includes a quick-start with clang and lld commands, and it reports that Propeller matches BOLT's gains with about 20% of its memory and time overhead on large benchmarks and SPEC 2017. A linked design document contains the detailed experiments. The page states the design and its experiments, but it does not report a final shipped result.
